description: A Single Mathematics B-style paper covering force along curves, coupled ODE modes, Parseval methods, harmonic functions, vector fields, ellipsoid scaling, and experimental errors.
instructions: Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Answers should be exact unless a numerical approximation is requested.
Begin each main question on a new page when working on paper.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: A particle has position \(\mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,2-t)\), for \(0\le t\le1\). A force field is given by \(\mathbf F(x,y,z)=(2x,y-z,x+z)\).
questions.title: Variable Force Along a Curve

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the velocity and the speed at \(t=1\).
parts.answer: Differentiate the position vector component by component: \[\mathbf v(t)=\mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t,-1).\] At \(t=1\), \[\mathbf v(1)=(1,2,-1).\] Therefore the speed is \[|\mathbf v(1)|=\sqrt{1^2+2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt6.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the acceleration and the net force if the particle has mass \(m\).
parts.answer: Differentiate velocity to get acceleration: \[\mathbf a(t)=\mathbf v'(t)=(0,2,0).\] For constant mass, Newton's second law gives \[\mathbf F_{\text{net}}=m\mathbf a=(0,2m,0).\] Thus the acceleration and net force are constant over the interval.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find \(\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf v(t)\).
parts.answer: Along the path, \(x=t\), \(y=t^2\), and \(z=2-t\). Hence \[\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=(2t,t^2-(2-t),t+2-t)=(2t,t^2+t-2,2).\] Dotting with \(\mathbf v(t)=(1,2t,-1)\), \[\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf v(t)=2t+2t(t^2+t-2)-2=2t^3+2t^2-2t-2.\]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the work done by \(\mathbf F\) along the path from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\).
parts.answer: The work along a parametrised path is \[W=\int_0^1\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf v(t)\,dt.\] Using part (c), \[W=\int_0^1(2t^3+2t^2-2t-2)\,dt.\] Therefore \[W=\left[\frac{t^4}{2}+\frac{2t^3}{3}-t^2-2t\right]_0^1=\frac12+\frac23-1-2=-\frac{11}{6}.\] The negative sign means the force removes energy along this path.

questions.stem: Two coupled displacements \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) satisfy \(x''=-5x+4y\) and \(y''=4x-5y\).
questions.title: Coupled Oscillator Modes

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Let \(p=x+y\) and \(q=x-y\). Show that the equations decouple into equations for \(p\) and \(q\).
parts.answer: Differentiate the definitions twice: \(p''=x''+y''\) and \(q''=x''-y''\). Using the coupled equations, \[p''=(-5x+4y)+(4x-5y)=-(x+y)=-p.\] Also \[q''=(-5x+4y)-(4x-5y)=-9x+9y=-9(x-y)=-9q.\] Hence the decoupled equations are \[p''+p=0,\qquad q''+9q=0.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: The initial conditions give \[p(0)=x(0)+y(0)=1,\qquad q(0)=x(0)-y(0)=1,\] and \[p'(0)=x'(0)+y'(0)=0,\qquad q'(0)=x'(0)-y'(0)=0.\] Solving \(p''+p=0\) gives \(p=A\cos t+B\sin t\). The initial conditions give \(p=\cos t\). Solving \(q''+9q=0\) gives \(q=C\cos3t+D\sin3t\), and the initial conditions give \(q=\cos3t\). Since \(x=(p+q)/2\) and \(y=(p-q)/2\), \[x(t)=\frac{\cos t+\cos3t}{2},\qquad y(t)=\frac{\cos t-\cos3t}{2}.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Interpret the two normal modes represented by \(p\) and \(q\).
parts.answer: The variable \(p=x+y\) measures the in-phase combination of the two displacements and oscillates with angular frequency \(1\). The variable \(q=x-y\) measures the out-of-phase combination and oscillates with angular frequency \(3\). The original motion is a superposition of these two normal modes.

questions.stem: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) for \(-2<x<2\), extended periodically with period \(4\).
questions.title: Even Quadratic On a Short Interval

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the Fourier coefficients of \(f\).
parts.answer: Here \(L=2\). The function is even, so \(b_n=0\) for all \(n\). The constant coefficient is \[a_0=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^Lx^2\,dx=\int_0^2x^2\,dx=\frac83.\] For \(n\ge1\), \[a_n=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^Lx^2\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx=\int_0^2x^2\cos\frac{n\pi x}{2}\,dx.\] With \(k=n\pi/2\), integration by parts twice gives \[\int_0^2x^2\cos kx\,dx=\frac{4(-1)^n}{k^2}.\] Since \(k^2=n^2\pi^2/4\), \[a_n=\frac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^2}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write the Fourier series and give the first four non-constant terms.
parts.answer: Since \(a_0/2=4/3\), the Fourier series is \[x^2\sim\frac43+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{16(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^2}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{2}.\] The first four non-constant terms are \[-\frac{16}{\pi^2}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}+\frac{4}{\pi^2}\cos(\pi x)-\frac{16}{9\pi^2}\cos\frac{3\pi x}{2}+\frac{1}{\pi^2}\cos(2\pi x).\] The alternating signs come from \((-1)^n\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use Parseval's theorem to evaluate \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^4\).
parts.answer: Parseval's theorem on \((-2,2)\) gives \[\frac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2}x^4\,dx=\frac{a_0^2}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n^2.\] The left side is \[\frac12\cdot2\int_0^2x^4\,dx=\frac{32}{5}.\] Also \(a_0^2/2=(8/3)^2/2=32/9\), and \(a_n^2=256/(n^4\pi^4)\). Therefore \[\frac{32}{5}=\frac{32}{9}+\frac{256}{\pi^4}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^4}.\] Rearranging gives \[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90}.\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that \(u\) satisfies Laplace's equation \(u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0\).
parts.answer: Differentiate \(u=x^2-y^2\) with respect to each variable. We have \[u_x=2x,\qquad u_{xx}=2,\] and \[u_y=-2y,\qquad u_{yy}=-2.\] Therefore \[u_{xx}+u_{yy}=2-2=0.\] Thus \(u\) is harmonic in the \((x,y)\)-plane.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find \(G(s,t)\), \(G_{ss}\), and \(G_{tt}\).
parts.answer: Substitute \(x=s+t\) and \(y=s-t\): \[G(s,t)=(s+t)^2-(s-t)^2.\] Expanding, \[(s+t)^2=s^2+2st+t^2,\qquad (s-t)^2=s^2-2st+t^2,\] so \[G(s,t)=4st.\] Therefore \[G_s=4t,\qquad G_{ss}=0,\] and \[G_t=4s,\qquad G_{tt}=0.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Does \(G\) satisfy \(G_{ss}+G_{tt}=0\)? Interpret the result for this example.
parts.answer: From part (b), \(G_{ss}=0\) and \(G_{tt}=0\). Hence \[G_{ss}+G_{tt}=0.\] In this example, the transformed function remains harmonic in the new variables. This conclusion follows directly from the transformed expression \(G=4st\), not from assuming that every coordinate change preserves the ordinary Laplacian.

questions.section: Section E: Critical Points and Vector Calculus
questions.title: Divergence, Curl, and Critical Surface

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find and classify the critical point of \(f\).
parts.answer: The first derivatives are \[f_x=2x-4,\qquad f_y=4y+8.\] Setting these equal to zero gives \(x=2\) and \(y=-2\). The Hessian is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}.\] Since both diagonal entries are positive and the determinant is \(8>0\), the Hessian is positive definite. Therefore \((2,-2)\) is a strict local minimum.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compute \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf W\) and \(\nabla\times\mathbf W\).
parts.answer:
Write \(\mathbf W=(P,Q,R)=(x^2y,yz,zx^2)\). The divergence is \[
abla\cdot\mathbf W=P_x+Q_y+R_z=2xy+z+x^2.\] The curl is \[
abla	imes\mathbf W=(R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).\] Since \(R_y=0\), \(Q_z=y\), \(P_z=0\), \(R_x=2xz\), \(Q_x=0\), and \(P_y=x^2\), \[
abla	imes\mathbf W=(-y,-2xz,-x^2).\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate the divergence and curl at \((1,1,1)\), and interpret the signs briefly.
parts.answer: At \((1,1,1)\), the divergence is \[2xy+z+x^2=2(1)(1)+1+1=4.\] This positive value indicates local source-like or net-outflow behaviour. The curl is \[(-y,-2xz,-x^2)=(-1,-2,-1).\] The non-zero curl indicates local rotational tendency, with direction given by \((-1,-2,-1)\) according to the right-hand-rule convention.

questions.section: Section F: Multiple Integrals and Vector Identities
questions.stem: Let \(E\) be the ellipsoid \(\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+\frac{z^2}{16}\le1\). Use the scaling \(x=2u\), \(y=3v\), and \(z=4w\).
questions.title: Ellipsoid Scaling

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the image of \(E\) in \((u,v,w)\)-coordinates and find the Jacobian scale factor.
parts.answer: Substituting \(x=2u\), \(y=3v\), and \(z=4w\) into the ellipsoid gives \[\frac{(2u)^2}{4}+\frac{(3v)^2}{9}+\frac{(4w)^2}{16}=u^2+v^2+w^2\le1.\] Thus \(E\) maps to the unit ball \(B:u^2+v^2+w^2\le1\). The Jacobian determinant of the scaling is \[\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|=2\cdot3\cdot4=24.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the volume of \(E\).
parts.answer: The unit ball has volume \(4\pi/3\). Since the scaling multiplies volumes by \(24\), \[\operatorname{Vol}(E)=24\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}=32\pi.\] This agrees with the ellipsoid formula \((4\pi/3)abc\), where \(a=2\), \(b=3\), and \(c=4\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\iiint_E x^2\,dV\).
parts.answer: Under the scaling, \(x^2=(2u)^2=4u^2\) and \(dV=24\,du\,dv\,dw\). Therefore \[\iiint_E x^2\,dV=96\iiint_Bu^2\,du\,dv\,dw.\] By symmetry in the unit ball, \[\iiint_Bu^2\,dV=\frac13\iiint_B(u^2+v^2+w^2)\,dV.\] In spherical coordinates on the unit ball, \[\iiint_B(u^2+v^2+w^2)\,dV=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1\rho^2\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\frac{4\pi}{5}.\] Hence \(\iiint_Bu^2\,dV=4\pi/15\), and so \[\iiint_E x^2\,dV=96\cdot\frac{4\pi}{15}=\frac{128\pi}{5}.\]

questions.stem: Two independent zero-mean measurement errors are modelled by \(E_1\sim N(0,0.04)\) and \(E_2\sim N(0,0.09)\). The combined error is \(E=E_1-E_2\).
questions.title: Experimental Error Audit

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the mean and variance of \(E\).
parts.answer: Using linearity of expectation, \[E[E]=E[E_1]-E[E_2]=0-0=0.\] Since the errors are independent, variances add under subtraction as well as addition: \[\operatorname{Var}(E)=\operatorname{Var}(E_1)+\operatorname{Var}(E_2)=0.04+0.09=0.13.\] Therefore \(E\sim N(0,0.13)\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Estimate \(P(|E|<0.5)\).
parts.answer: The standard deviation of \(E\) is \(\sqrt{0.13}\approx0.361\). Standardising, \[P(|E|<0.5)=P\left(\left|Z\right|<\frac{0.5}{\sqrt{0.13}}\right)\approx P(|Z|<1.39).\] From standard normal tables, \(\Phi(1.39)\approx0.9177\). Therefore \[P(|E|<0.5)\approx2(0.9177)-1=0.8354.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For \(25\) independent repetitions of the combined error, estimate \(P(|\bar E|<0.1)\).
parts.answer: The sample mean has mean \(0\) and variance \[\frac{0.13}{25}=0.0052.\] Its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.13}/5\approx0.0721\). Therefore \[P(|\bar E|<0.1)\approx P\left(|Z|<\frac{0.1}{0.0721}\right)=P(|Z|<1.39).\] Using the same table value as in part (b), this is approximately \[2(0.9177)-1=0.8354.\]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why independence matters in part (a), and describe the effect of adding a systematic offset \(b\).
parts.answer: Independence matters because it justifies adding the variances without a covariance term. If the errors were dependent, \(\operatorname{Var}(E_1-E_2)\) would also involve \(-2\operatorname{Cov}(E_1,E_2)\). A systematic offset \(b\) would shift the model to \(E+b\), changing the mean from \(0\) to \(b\), but it would not change the variance.
